title: QUIZ - 75
description: Test your knowledge, strengthen your reasoning, and learn something new with every question.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the correct syntax for calling a function with a given input
questions.question: In both mathematical notation and most programming languages, which of the following correctly calls the function h with input 50?
questions.explanation: Both mathematical and programming notation place the input in parentheses immediately after the function's name: h(50).
questions.hint: The function name comes first, followed by the input in parentheses.

questions.concept: Differences Between Mathematical and Programming Functions
questions.learningObjective: Identify a key difference between mathematical functions and general programming functions
questions.question: How can a programming function differ from a strict mathematical function?

options.label: A
options.text: A programming function may have side effects, such as printing output or modifying external state.

options.label: B
options.text: A programming function must return exactly the value 0.

options.label: C
options.text: A programming function cannot accept any parameters.

options.label: D
options.text: A programming function must always be linear.

questions.explanation: Unlike a pure mathematical function, a programming function can perform side effects (like printing, writing to a file, or changing a variable outside itself) in addition to returning a value.
questions.hint: Consider what programming functions can do besides simply computing and returning a value.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a pseudocode function has side effects beyond returning a computed value
questions.question:
Does the following pseudocode function have a side effect (behavior beyond returning a value based only on its input)? function g(x):
    log_to_file(x)
    return 9 * x

options.label: A
options.text: It has a side effect only if the input is negative.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, it has a side effect.

options.label: C
options.text: This cannot be determined from pseudocode alone.

options.label: D
options.text: No, it is a pure function with no side effects.

questions.explanation: This function does more than compute and return a value: it also prints, logs, or modifies external state, which is a side effect.
questions.hint: A side effect is anything the function does besides computing and returning a value from its input.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the shared property of determinism between mathematical and programming functions
questions.question: Which behavior do mathematical functions and pure programming functions have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: It must always return a value between 0 and 1.

options.label: B
options.text: It must take exactly zero arguments.

options.label: C
options.text: Given the same input, it should always produce the same output.

options.label: D
options.text: It must modify a global variable every time it is called.

questions.explanation: Both mathematical functions and pure programming functions are deterministic: the same input always produces the same output.
questions.hint: Think about determinism: does the function behave consistently for a repeated input?

questions.learningObjective: Translate a mathematical function definition into an equivalent pseudocode function
questions.question: Which pseudocode function correctly implements the mathematical function \( f(t) = 5t - 5 \)?

options.label: A
options.text:
function f(t):
    print(5 * t - 5)

options.label: B
options.text:
function f(t):
    return 5 * t - 5

options.label: C
options.text:
function f(t):
    return 5 + t - 5

options.label: D
options.text:
function f(t):
    t = 5 * t - 5

questions.explanation: A correct implementation multiplies the input by 5, then subtracts 5, and returns the result, matching \( f(t) = 5t - 5 \).
questions.hint: The pseudocode must compute the same expression as the mathematical formula and explicitly return the result.
